4PW model specification

49 variables · 66 causal links · 24 stock–flow connections · 35 named loops

Public rendering of the latest researcher-supplied specification used by these slides. It preserves the ordered walk, labels, polarity, delays and mechanism statements. This is a proposed programme theory, not an independently validated causal model.

The 16 added causal links are analogical proposals. Their supporting 42-loop dossier is not supplied here. Stock–flow identities are accounting relations; prior-ledger records and structural closure do not constitute new causal validation.

The exact loop sequence

1. R1 · Taking Part Pays Off: Influence, Delivery and Trust Reinforce Each Other

การมีส่วนร่วมที่ได้ผลจริงเสริมแรงอิทธิพล การนำไปปฏิบัติ และความไว้วางใจ

Stage 1 · Voice · R · 2 negative signs · 3 delayed links

  1. INCLUSION AND EQUITY OF PARTICIPATION ACROSS POPULATION GROUPS → (+) uptake of proposals into decisions L02

    When participation includes more groups ↑, proposals carry more of the public's and the frontline's experience, so decisions fit conditions better and uptake of proposals can rise ↑.

  2. uptake of proposals into decisions → (+) INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

  3. INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS → (+) resolution implementation L05 · delay //

    When public and civil-society input shapes more decisions ↑, ministries build resolutions into strategies, pilots and budgets, so more resolutions are carried out and the backlog falls ↓, after a long delay.

  4. resolution implementation → (−) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED Stock–flow identity

    The outflow drains the stock: the more that flows out, the lower the stock.

  5. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (+) trust erosion L09 · delay //

    When the backlog of unimplemented resolutions grows ↑, participants see little return on their effort, so trust erosion rises ↑ and their trust that government will respond falls ↓, after a delay.

  6. trust erosion → (−) PARTICIPANTS' TRUST THAT GOVERNMENT WILL RESPOND Stock–flow identity

    The outflow drains the stock: the more that flows out, the lower the stock.

  7. PARTICIPANTS' TRUST THAT GOVERNMENT WILL RESPOND → (+) civil-society capacity development L10 · delay //

    When trust that government will respond is high ↑, civil-society groups keep investing in the assembly channel, so civil-society capacity development rises ↑, after a delay.

  8. civil-society capacity development → (+) CIVIL-SOCIETY CAPACITY FOR MEANINGFUL PARTICIPATION Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

  9. CIVIL-SOCIETY CAPACITY FOR MEANINGFUL PARTICIPATION → (+) joining of under-represented groups L11

    Two pathways run from civil-society capacity to inclusion.

  10. joining of under-represented groups → (+) INCLUSION AND EQUITY OF PARTICIPATION ACROSS POPULATION GROUPS Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

Influence helps resolutions get implemented; implementation builds trust, civil-society capacity and inclusive participation, which raise influence again.

2. R2 · Rushed Decisions Narrow Voice and Leave More Resolutions Unimplemented

การเร่งตัดสินใจทำให้เสียงประชาชนแคบลงและมติค้างมากขึ้น

Stage 1 · Voice · R · 2 negative signs · 1 delayed links

  1. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (+) time pressure on policy decisions L17

    When the backlog of unimplemented resolutions grows ↑, past resolutions compete with new items for assembly and committee time and for the same few committee members, so the time available for each decision shrinks and time pressure on policy decisions rises ↑.

  2. time pressure on policy decisions → (−) joining of under-represented groups L18

    When time pressure on policy decisions rises ↑, preparation and consultation windows shrink, groups outside the usual channels have too little time to organise and contribute, and urgent or political decisions take routes that skip consultation, so inclusion and equity fall ↓.

  3. joining of under-represented groups → (+) INCLUSION AND EQUITY OF PARTICIPATION ACROSS POPULATION GROUPS Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

  4. INCLUSION AND EQUITY OF PARTICIPATION ACROSS POPULATION GROUPS → (+) uptake of proposals into decisions L02

    When participation includes more groups ↑, proposals carry more of the public's and the frontline's experience, so decisions fit conditions better and uptake of proposals can rise ↑.

  5. uptake of proposals into decisions → (+) INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

  6. INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS → (+) resolution implementation L05 · delay //

    When public and civil-society input shapes more decisions ↑, ministries build resolutions into strategies, pilots and budgets, so more resolutions are carried out and the backlog falls ↓, after a long delay.

  7. resolution implementation → (−) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED Stock–flow identity

    The outflow drains the stock: the more that flows out, the lower the stock.

A growing backlog adds time pressure, which narrows who takes part, so influence and implementation fall and the backlog grows.

Stage 1 · Voice · B · 1 negative signs · 0 delayed links

  1. time pressure on policy decisions → (+) resolution implementation L19

    When time pressure on policy decisions rises ↑ and the deadline comes with an owner and money, agencies act quickly, so implementation of the resolution rises ↑ in the short term.

  2. resolution implementation → (−) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED Stock–flow identity

    The outflow drains the stock: the more that flows out, the lower the stock.

  3. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (+) time pressure on policy decisions L17

4. B11 · When the Assembly Route Fails, Demands Take the Political Fast Track

เมื่อเส้นทางสมัชชาไม่ได้ผล ข้อเรียกร้องหันไปใช้ช่องทางลัดทางการเมือง

Stage 1 · Voice · B · 1 negative signs · 0 delayed links

  1. INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS → (−) use of the political fast track for benefit demands AA1

    When citizen benefit proposals stall behind the evidence bar of the benefit-package process ↓, a demand can still become a decision if politicians take it up, so use of the political fast track rises ↑.

  2. use of the political fast track for benefit demands → (+) uptake of proposals into decisions AA2

    When a demand is taken up through the political fast track ↑ (a minister-chaired purchaser board or a Cabinet decision), it becomes a decision quickly and can bypass the cost-effectiveness test, so uptake of that demand rises ↑.

  3. uptake of proposals into decisions → (+) INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

When influence through the assembly route is low, demands move to the political fast track, which turns them into decisions quickly.

5. B2 · Follow-Up Carries Proposals Into Decisions

การติดตามช่วยผลักข้อเสนอเข้าสู่การตัดสินใจ

Stage 2 · Decision · B · 1 negative signs · 2 delayed links

  1. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (+) intensity of corrective follow-up L12 · delay //

    When the backlog grows ↑, complaints and stalled implementation lead the commission to create, reorganise and plan follow-up bodies, so total corrective follow-up intensifies ↑, after a delay; but follow-up is rationed by priority, so each resolution in a lower tier receives less.

  2. intensity of corrective follow-up → (+) uptake of proposals into decisions L04

    When corrective follow-up is more intense ↑ and carries authority (high-level coordination, a place among the agency's own indicators), more proposals are pressed onto decision-makers' agendas, so uptake into decisions rises ↑; routine follow-up letters alone produce reports, not decisions.

  3. uptake of proposals into decisions → (+) INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS Stock–flow identity

    The inflow fills the stock.

  4. INFLUENCE OF PUBLIC AND CIVIL-SOCIETY INPUT ON POLICY DECISIONS → (+) resolution implementation L05 · delay //

    When public and civil-society input shapes more decisions ↑, ministries build resolutions into strategies, pilots and budgets, so more resolutions are carried out and the backlog falls ↓, after a long delay.

  5. resolution implementation → (−) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED Stock–flow identity

    The outflow drains the stock: the more that flows out, the lower the stock.

Follow-up raises the uptake of proposals into decisions, which raises implementation.

6. B1 · Case-by-Case Follow-Up Clears the Backlog in the Short Term

การตามแก้รายกรณีช่วยลดมติค้างในระยะสั้น (ทำงานหนักขึ้น)

Stage 5 · Institutionalisation · B · 1 negative signs · 1 delayed links

  1. intensity of corrective follow-up → (+) resolution implementation L13

    When corrective follow-up intensifies ↑, the follow-up committee keeps sectors cooperating and secures commitment, so stalled resolutions are pushed into implementation and the backlog falls ↓; this holds where interests align and fails where strong interests oppose the resolution or follow-up is only a letter.

  2. resolution implementation → (−) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED Stock–flow identity

    The outflow drains the stock: the more that flows out, the lower the stock.

  3. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (+) intensity of corrective follow-up L12 · delay //

    When the backlog grows ↑, complaints and stalled implementation lead the commission to create, reorganise and plan follow-up bodies, so total corrective follow-up intensifies ↑, after a delay; but follow-up is rationed by priority, so each resolution in a lower tier receives less.

A growing backlog triggers case-by-case follow-up, which speeds implementation.

7. B13 · Counting Activity as Progress Shrinks the Backlog on Paper

นับกิจกรรมเป็นความคืบหน้า มติค้างจึงลดลงแค่บนกระดาษ

Stage 4 · Monitoring and learning · B · 1 negative signs · 0 delayed links

  1. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (−) stringency of the standard for counting a resolution as implemented L30

    When the backlog of unimplemented resolutions grows ↑ (69 in 2016, 77 in 2018, 96 in 2024), the follow-up committees regroup it to focus their work: they merge related resolutions, drop from follow-up those that existing mechanisms already carry, only watch those judged to be moving, report on some only when a major change occurs, give priority to quick wins and to issues likely to succeed, and end reporting on others without counting them achieved, so the stringency of the standard applied when a resolution leaves follow-up falls ↓.

  2. stringency of the standard for counting a resolution as implemented → (+) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED L31

    When the standard for counting a resolution as implemented is stricter ↑, fewer resolutions are closed without delivery, so more remain in the backlog ↑; when it is relaxed, the backlog shrinks on paper without any change on the ground.

A growing backlog lowers the practical bar for counting a resolution as implemented, so the backlog shrinks on paper at once, without delivery.

8. B14 · Softened Formal Targets Lower the Bar for Implementation

เป้าหมายทางการที่ถูกผ่อนลงทำให้เกณฑ์การนำไปปฏิบัติต่ำลง

Stage 5 · Institutionalisation · B · 1 negative signs · 1 delayed links

  1. RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED → (−) stringency of formal implementation targets in resolutions and plans L32 · delay //

    When a resolution stays unimplemented for years ↑, it is proposed for revisiting, and the revised resolution sets later deadlines, taken from the implementing ministry's own timetable, so the stringency of formal implementation targets falls ↓, after a delay of several years: the asbestos resolution's targets of 2011–2012 (2010) became deadlines of 2022 and 2025 (2019).

  2. stringency of formal implementation targets in resolutions and plans → (+) stringency of the standard for counting a resolution as implemented L33

    When formal targets are stricter, dated and specific ↑, the commission's own report and evaluators judge resolutions against those terms, so the practical standard for counting a resolution as implemented is stricter ↑; when targets are counts of policies, qualitative or without a timeframe, progress is counted as activity, self-assessment or hand-over.

  3. stringency of the standard for counting a resolution as implemented → (+) RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IMPLEMENTED L31

    When the standard for counting a resolution as implemented is stricter ↑, fewer resolutions are closed without delivery, so more remain in the backlog ↑; when it is relaxed, the backlog shrinks on paper without any change on the ground.

A persistent backlog softens or postpones the formal targets in resolutions and plans after a delay, which lowers the practical bar in turn.

16. R11 · Reporting Work Erodes Capacity and Disengages Budget Holders

ภาระรายงานกัดกร่อนขีดความสามารถและทำให้ผู้ถืองบถอยห่าง

Stage 4 · Monitoring and learning · R · 2 negative signs · 2 delayed links

  1. PUBLIC-SECTOR CAPACITY TO SUPPORT PARTICIPATION AND ACT ON ITS PROPOSALS → (+) engagement of budget holders L07

    When public-sector capacity is higher ↑, coordinating agencies have the staff and skills to work across ministries and to present usable local data, so they can bring budget holders in early, and budget holders with stronger capacity of their own take on funding roles, so engagement of budget holders rises ↑.

  2. engagement of budget holders → (+) implementation readiness of decisions L06a

    When budget holders take part in deliberation ↑, from the drafting stage onwards, decisions arrive with owners, money and a place in the agency's indicators, so implementation readiness rises ↑.

Externally set drivers

The supplied specification lists these variables as having no cause inside this model. This is a boundary of the model, not a claim that they lack causes in reality.

  • withdrawal of participants
  • decay of influence
  • resolution adoption
  • civil-society capacity loss
  • lapse of adopted improvements
  • openness of forums to new and under-represented groups
  • relaxation of restrictive practices

Comparison with the retained source ledger

49 of the 50 original ledger endpoint/sign signatures match the revised specification. AA5 changes its target to adoption of restrictive practices. The earlier simplified diagram was a separate graphic projection; its 28 restored signatures are not 28 changes to the underlying evidence ledger.

This comparison checks identity and provenance. It does not reappraise causal evidence, saturation, source independence or transferability. AA1–AA4 have a wider informal-routes interpretation than the political-fast-track evidence; stock-based persistence of provider restriction remains a hypothesis.

ChangeElementWhy

Five breaks

BreakLoops added by the revision
1. Voice without influenceR15, R18, R19, R20: deliberative quality and informal routes now explain why voice does not become influence
2. Decisions without implementable commitmentR18: inclusion makes decisions more workable
3. Mandates without sustainable capacityB12 now runs through a stock of restrictive practice, so restriction persists after overload eases
4. Transparency without usable learningR16, R17, R19: defensiveness limits the usability of information, and responsive government renews deliberation
5. Adaptation without institutional changeR20, R21: informal routes and working harder both crowd out rule learning

Dynamic hypotheses

Dynamic hypothesisChange
TranslationInfluence also depends on the quality of deliberation, which makes shared information usable (N05) and government responses transparent (N16).
ErosionA second path of erosion runs through deliberation: time pressure and a defensive climate erode deliberative norms (R15, R17).
CeilingThe ceiling now holds even when deliberation is good, rather than whatever its quality: capacity and resources still cap readiness.
LearningWorking harder on overload (R21) and informal routes (R20) are two further ways in which quick responses crowd out rule learning.

Scope and qualifications

  • The evidence for the 16 new links comes from the 42-loop dossier, which studied health-coverage implementation more than 4PW resolutions, so each new link carries the status analogous until mechanism-targeted searches find 4PW evidence.
  • The assignment of dossier variables to model elements is the author's reading and should be checked by the researcher.
  • Widening the informal-routes converter widens the scope of links AA1 to AA4, whose evidence concerns the political fast track only.
  • Mindsets from the dossier are not variables here; they belong in the reasoning half of each link's mechanism (dossier_vs_canonical_revision.md, section 5).

Original source files, consultation transcripts and participant-level records are not distributed by this reader.
